gloss: A doctor who treats animals.
examples: I'm taking the cat to the *vet* on Friday.
Our *vet* says he needs to lose five pounds.
Both *vets* in town were booked solid.
contrast: In American English *vet* is also short for veteran, a former soldier; only the context tells you which.

gloss: A person qualified to treat sick or injured animals.
examples: She's studying to be a *veterinarian*.
The *veterinarian* put six stitches in his paw.
Three *veterinarians* work out of that clinic.
contrast: Americans say veterinarian; the British usually say vet or veterinary surgeon.

gloss: The branch of medicine that deals with animal health.
examples: He went into *veterinary medicine* after college.
The school of *veterinary medicine* is on the north campus.
*Veterinary medicine* has changed a lot in twenty years.

gloss: A clinic where sick or injured animals are treated.
examples: There's a 24-hour *animal hospital* off the highway.
We rushed her to the *animal hospital* at midnight.
Both *animal hospitals* were closed on Sunday.

gloss: A shop that sells animals and supplies for them.
examples: He bought the hamster at a *pet store* in the mall.
The *pet store* sells live crickets for lizards.
Two *pet stores* closed downtown last year.
contrast: American *pet store*; the British say pet shop.

gloss: Food made for animals kept at home.
examples: *Pet food* has gotten expensive.
We buy *pet food* in bulk twice a year.
The recall covered several brands of *pet food*.
contrast: Uncountable: say a bag of *pet food*, never 'a pet food'.

gloss: Food made for dogs.
examples: We're out of *dog food* again.
She mixes wet *dog food* into his kibble.
A bag of *dog food* costs thirty dollars now.

gloss: Food made for cats.
examples: The *cat food* is under the sink.
He opened a can of *cat food* and she came running.
Pick up some *cat food* while you're out.

gloss: Dry pet food shaped into small hard pieces.
examples: He gets a cup of *kibble* twice a day.
The puppy won't touch dry *kibble*.
There's *kibble* all over the kitchen floor.
contrast: Uncountable: a cup of *kibble*, not 'a kibble'.

gloss: A small piece of tasty food given to an animal as a reward.
examples: Give him a *treat* when he sits.
She keeps *treats* in her coat pocket.
One more *treat* and that's it for tonight.

gloss: A tough toy made for a dog to bite and chew on.
examples: The puppy destroyed his new *chew toy* in an hour.
Get her a rubber *chew toy* instead of a shoe.
There are *chew toys* under every couch cushion.

gloss: A strap or cord clipped to a collar to keep a dog under control.
examples: Keep your dog on a *leash* in the park.
He grabbed the *leash* and the dog went crazy.
Both *leashes* were tangled together.
contrast: American *leash*; the British say lead.

gloss: A set of straps that goes around an animal's chest and shoulders.
examples: A *harness* is easier on his neck than a collar.
She clipped the leash to his *harness*.
The store had *harnesses* in three sizes.

gloss: A small metal disc on a collar with the owner's contact details.
examples: His *dog tag* has our phone number on it.
The *dog tag* jingles whenever he moves.
Order two *dog tags* in case one falls off.
contrast: *Dog tags* is also the everyday name for the metal ID tags a US soldier wears.

gloss: A small shelter outdoors for a dog to sleep in.
examples: He built a *doghouse* out of scrap lumber.
The old *doghouse* is falling apart.
Both *doghouses* need new roofs.
contrast: American *doghouse* is the British kennel; 'in the doghouse' also means in trouble with someone.

gloss: A small box or bag with air holes for carrying an animal.
examples: The cat hates going in the *pet carrier*.
Airlines have size limits for *pet carriers*.
Put a towel in the *pet carrier* so she's comfortable.

gloss: A shallow tray filled with grains where a cat relieves itself indoors.
examples: The *litter box* needs to be cleaned.
We keep the *litter box* in the laundry room.
Two cats really need two *litter boxes*.
contrast: American *litter box*; the British say litter tray.

gloss: Absorbent grains poured into a tray for a cat to use.
examples: Pick up a bag of *cat litter*.
*Cat litter* tracks all over the house.
This *cat litter* is supposed to control odor.

gloss: A covered upright post a cat can dig its claws into.
examples: She sharpens her claws on the *scratching post*.
Get him a *scratching post* before he ruins the couch.
We have *scratching posts* in two rooms.

gloss: A tall carpeted structure with platforms for a cat to climb and sleep on.
examples: The gray cat sleeps on top of the *cat tree*.
We put the *cat tree* by the window.
Those *cat trees* are surprisingly expensive.

gloss: A minty herb whose smell excites most cats.
examples: A little *catnip* makes him roll around like a kitten.
The toy is stuffed with dried *catnip*.
*Catnip* has no effect on some cats at all.

gloss: A glass container of water where fish are kept.
examples: The *fish tank* needs cleaning.
He keeps a ten-gallon *fish tank* in his room.
Both *fish tanks* have heaters.

gloss: A round glass bowl for keeping a fish or two.
examples: The goldfish swims in circles around the *fishbowl*.
Don't put the *fishbowl* in direct sunlight.
Those glass *fishbowls* crack easily.

gloss: Dried flakes or pellets fed to fish in a tank.
examples: Sprinkle a little *fish food* on the surface.
We're almost out of *fish food*.
Too much *fish food* fouls the water.

gloss: The work of washing, brushing and trimming an animal's coat.
examples: Long-haired cats need regular *grooming*.
*Grooming* costs more than I expected.
His *grooming* takes about two hours.

gloss: Someone whose job is washing and trimming pets.
examples: Our *groomer* cut his nails too short.
She works as a dog *groomer* downtown.
The *groomers* are booked through the holidays.

gloss: The natural loss of hair from an animal's coat.
examples: *Shedding* gets worse in the spring.
This brush cuts down on *shedding*.
There's no way to stop the *shedding* completely.

gloss: Tiny flakes of skin from an animal that often cause allergies.
examples: My sister is allergic to cat *dander*.
*Dander* collects in the carpet.
An air filter helps with pet *dander*.

gloss: A wad of swallowed hair that a cat coughs up.
examples: The cat coughed up a *hairball* on the rug.
*Hairballs* are common in long-haired breeds.
There's special food that prevents *hairballs*.

gloss: A collar treated with chemicals that kill fleas.
examples: We put a *flea collar* on both dogs.
The *flea collar* smells awful.
*Flea collars* work for about six months.

gloss: A medicine put on an animal to kill or keep off fleas.
examples: The vet recommended a monthly *flea treatment*.
She applies the *flea treatment* between his shoulder blades.
Some *flea treatments* kill ticks too.

gloss: Treating an animal with medicine that kills intestinal worms.
examples: The puppy is due for *deworming*.
*Deworming* is part of the first vet visit.
Regular *deworming* keeps the whole litter healthy.

gloss: An operation that makes a female animal unable to have young.
examples: The shelter covers the cost of *spaying*.
*Spaying* is usually done before six months.
She scheduled the *spaying* for next week.

gloss: An operation that makes a male animal unable to father young.
examples: *Neutering* calmed him down a lot.
The clinic offers low-cost *neutering*.
They require *neutering* before adoption.
contrast: Americans say NOO-tur-ing; the British say NYOO-tur-ing.

gloss: Surgically removing a cat's claws.
examples: *Declawing* is banned in several cities.
Most vets refuse to do *declawing* now.
She chose nail caps instead of *declawing*.

gloss: A repeat injection that keeps an earlier vaccine working.
examples: He's due for a *booster shot* in March.
The *booster shot* costs about forty dollars.
Puppies need several *booster shots* the first year.

gloss: A contagious dog illness that causes a harsh, dry cough.
examples: The whole shelter came down with *kennel cough*.
*Kennel cough* sounds like a honking goose.
He caught *kennel cough* at doggy daycare.
contrast: The gh in cough sounds like f: KAWF.

gloss: A serious viral disease of dogs and some other animals.
examples: The puppy was vaccinated against *distemper*.
*Distemper* is often fatal in young dogs.
The shelter had an outbreak of *distemper* last winter.

gloss: A skin disease caused by mites that makes an animal's hair fall out.
examples: The stray had *mange* on his back and ears.
*Mange* is caused by tiny mites burrowing in the skin.
Medicated baths cleared up the *mange*.

gloss: A contagious skin infection that leaves round bald patches.
examples: The kitten came home with *ringworm*.
*Ringworm* spreads to people, so wash your hands.
It took a month to get rid of the *ringworm*.
contrast: *Ringworm* is a fungus, not a worm.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: A parasitic worm carried by mosquitoes that lives in a dog's heart and lungs.
examples: Give him the *heartworm* pill on the first of the month.
The dog tested positive for *heartworm*.
*Heartworms* can grow up to a foot long.
contrast: Countable for the worms themselves; uncountable for the disease: tested positive for *heartworm*.

gloss: Painlessly ending the life of a hopelessly sick animal.
examples: The vet talked us through *euthanasia*.
*Euthanasia* is never an easy decision.
The clinic charges separately for *euthanasia*.

gloss: A policy that pays part of an animal's medical bills.
examples: We finally bought *pet insurance*.
*Pet insurance* covered most of the surgery.
Read what the *pet insurance* actually pays for.

gloss: The city department that picks up stray and dangerous animals.
examples: Somebody called *animal control* about the loose dog.
*Animal control* picked up the raccoon in our attic.
*Animal control* holds strays for two weeks.

gloss: The good treatment and comfort of animals.
examples: She volunteers for an *animal welfare* group.
The law raised *animal welfare* standards on farms.
*Animal welfare* was the main issue in the campaign.

gloss: A place that takes in homeless animals and finds homes for them.
examples: We adopted him from the *animal shelter*.
The *animal shelter* is full again.
Both *animal shelters* need foster homes.

gloss: A charity that rescues animals and works against cruelty to them.
examples: The *humane society* runs a low-cost clinic.
She donates to the local *humane society* every year.
Several *humane societies* took in animals after the fire.
contrast: *Humane* is stressed on the second syllable, hyoo-MAYN, unlike human.

gloss: A long-handled scoop for picking up dog waste.
examples: Bring a *pooper scooper* to the dog park.
He keeps a *pooper scooper* in the trunk.
The park provides bags but no *pooper scoopers*.

gloss: A small plastic bag for picking up after a dog.
examples: Take a *poop bag* with you.
The dispenser was out of *poop bags*.
She tied the *poop bag* shut and dropped it in the can.

gloss: A fenced public area where dogs can run without a leash.
examples: We take him to the *dog park* every morning.
The *dog park* has a separate side for small dogs.
There are three *dog parks* in the city.

gloss: Someone paid to take other people's dogs out for walks.
examples: We hired a *dog walker* for weekday afternoons.
The *dog walker* handles six dogs at once.
Good *dog walkers* book up fast.
contrast: The l in walker is silent: WAW-kur.

gloss: Someone paid to look after an animal while its owner is away.
examples: A *pet sitter* stays at the house while we travel.
Our *pet sitter* sends photos every day.
She works weekends as a *pet sitter*.

gloss: A business that looks after dogs during the working day.
examples: He goes to *doggy daycare* three days a week.
The *doggy daycare* has a webcam.
There are two *doggy daycares* near the office.

gloss: An animal's readiness to do what it is told.
examples: The dog has no *obedience* at all.
We're working on basic *obedience*.
*Obedience* takes daily practice.
contrast: Stressed on the second syllable: oh-BEE-dee-uhns.

gloss: A class where dogs are taught to follow commands.
examples: We sent the puppy to *obedience school*.
*Obedience school* meets on Tuesday nights.
Both *obedience schools* had waiting lists.

gloss: Teaching a young animal to relieve itself outdoors.
examples: *Housebreaking* a puppy takes patience.
We're still in the middle of *housebreaking*.
Crate training helps with *housebreaking*.
contrast: In legal English *housebreaking* means breaking into a house; the pet sense is a separate word.

gloss: A game in which a dog runs after a thrown object and brings it back.
examples: He'll play *fetch* until he collapses.
We threw the ball and played *fetch* for an hour.
*Fetch* is the only game she cares about.

gloss: A whistle pitched so high that dogs hear it and people barely do.
examples: The trainer blew a *dog whistle* we couldn't hear.
He carries a *dog whistle* on his key ring.
*Dog whistles* work above the range of human hearing.
contrast: The t in whistle is silent: WIS-uhl. In politics a *dog whistle* is also a coded message.

gloss: A person who keeps an animal at home.
examples: Every *pet owner* on the block got the notice.
*Pet owners* have to clean up after their dogs.
As a *pet owner*, you're responsible for the vaccinations.

gloss: A person who controls and works with a trained animal.
examples: The *handler* led the dog around the ring.
Police dogs live with their *handlers*.
She's been a *handler* at dog shows for years.

gloss: A competition where dogs are judged against their breed standard.
examples: They won best in breed at the *dog show*.
The *dog show* is at the fairgrounds this weekend.
He judges *dog shows* around the country.

gloss: A place that breeds puppies for profit in bad conditions.
examples: The dogs were rescued from a *puppy mill*.
Never buy from a *puppy mill*.
The state shut down two *puppy mills* last year.

gloss: A group of animals of one species with the same fixed appearance and traits.
examples: What *breed* is she?
That *breed* needs a lot of exercise.
Some flat-faced *breeds* have breathing problems.

gloss: A person who keeps animals in order to produce young from them.
examples: We got him from a *breeder* in Ohio.
A good *breeder* will show you both parents.
*Breeders* keep records going back generations.

gloss: The keeping of animals so that they produce young.
examples: *Breeding* season starts in the spring.
She retired the mare from *breeding*.
Careful *breeding* reduces hereditary disease.

gloss: An animal whose parents are both of the same breed.
examples: He's a *purebred*, with papers and everything.
*Purebreds* often cost thousands of dollars.
The shelter had one *purebred* among forty mutts.

gloss: An animal whose parents are of two different breeds.
examples: The dog is a *crossbreed* of a poodle and a lab.
*Crossbreeds* are often healthier than purebreds.
That *crossbreed* got the best of both breeds.
contrast: The noun is stressed on the first syllable, KRAWSS-breed; as a verb the stress moves to the second.

gloss: A dog of no particular breed.
examples: He's just a *mutt* from the pound.
*Mutts* make great family dogs.
Our *mutt* is part shepherd and part who knows what.

gloss: A dog of mixed and unknown breeding.
examples: The old *mongrel* followed us home.
*Mongrels* were once looked down on at shows.
She adopted a scruffy brown *mongrel*.

gloss: A written record of an animal's ancestors.
examples: The breeder showed us the puppy's *pedigree*.
His *pedigree* goes back four generations.
*Pedigrees* are registered with the kennel club.

gloss: The smallest and weakest animal in a litter.
examples: The *runt* of the litter is always the smallest.
Nobody wanted the *runt*, so we took him.
*Runts* often need extra feeding at first.

gloss: Any of several small, bold breeds of dog bred to hunt animals in burrows.
examples: That *terrier* barks at everything.
*Terriers* were bred to hunt rats.
She has a wire-haired *terrier*.

gloss: A breed of gundog trained to bring back shot birds.
examples: A golden *retriever* is good with kids.
The *retriever* brought the stick right back.
*Retrievers* love the water.

gloss: A breed of dog with thick curly hair, often clipped in patterns.
examples: Her *poodle* just came back from the groomer.
*Poodles* don't shed much.
The standard *poodle* is much bigger than the toy.

gloss: A heavy short-legged breed with a wide flat face.
examples: The *bulldog* snores louder than my father.
*Bulldogs* overheat easily in summer.
He walks a stocky brown *bulldog* every evening.

gloss: A small hunting hound with drooping ears and a loud bark.
examples: The *beagle* followed the scent across the yard.
*Beagles* have a loud, carrying bark.
We named the *beagle* after a cartoon dog.

gloss: A breed of long-nosed sheepdog with a thick coat.
examples: The *collie* herded the kids into the corner.
*Collies* need a job to do.
A border *collie* is the smartest dog I've owned.

gloss: A breed of dog with a long body and very short legs.
examples: The *dachshund* can't handle stairs anymore.
*Dachshunds* were bred to hunt badgers.
Their *dachshund* is shaped like a hot dog.
contrast: A German loanword: DAHKS-huund. Many Americans just say wiener dog.

gloss: A small breed of dog with a flat wrinkled face and a curled tail.
examples: The *pug* wheezes when he gets excited.
*Pugs* have a lot of breathing problems.
She dressed the *pug* in a sweater.

gloss: A thick-coated northern breed bred to pull sleds.
examples: A *husky* needs cold weather and a lot of running.
*Huskies* howl instead of barking.
The *husky* has one blue eye and one brown.
contrast: Also an adjective meaning big and sturdy, or a voice that sounds rough.

gloss: A tall, very fast breed of dog with a narrow body.
examples: The *greyhound* can outrun a bicycle.
Retired racing *greyhounds* make calm pets.
The *greyhound* sleeps twenty hours a day.

gloss: A breed of dog with long silky ears and a wavy coat.
examples: The *spaniel* has long, silky ears.
*Spaniels* were bred to flush birds out of cover.
Their cocker *spaniel* is nine years old.

gloss: A dog trained to control and move a flock of sheep.
examples: The *sheepdog* moved the whole flock alone.
*Sheepdogs* work off whistle commands.
An old *sheepdog* lay by the gate.

gloss: A small herding breed with short legs and large upright ears.
examples: The *corgi* has short legs and no patience.
*Corgis* shed constantly.
She posts pictures of her *corgi* every day.

gloss: A large hound with a superb sense of smell, used for tracking.
examples: The *bloodhound* tracked him three miles.
*Bloodhounds* have the best noses of any breed.
Police brought in a *bloodhound*.
contrast: Blood is pronounced BLUHD, rhyming with mud.

gloss: A small dog kept purely as company.
examples: The little *lapdog* never leaves her side.
*Lapdogs* were bred for company, not work.
He's a sixty-pound *lapdog* in his own mind.

gloss: A dog kept to bark a warning when strangers come.
examples: They keep a *watchdog* at the lot.
*Watchdogs* bark at anything that moves.
The *watchdog* woke the whole street.
contrast: A *watchdog* is also a group that keeps an eye on a government or an industry.

gloss: A dog trained to protect a place or a person.
examples: A *guard dog* patrols the warehouse at night.
*Guard dogs* are trained not to take food from strangers.
The sign warns about a *guard dog*.

gloss: A dog trained to lead a blind person safely.
examples: His *guide dog* is a yellow lab.
*Guide dogs* are allowed in restaurants.
The *guide dog* stopped at the curb.

gloss: A dog trained to do specific tasks for a person with a disability.
examples: Her *service dog* wears a vest in public.
*Service dogs* can go anywhere their handler goes.
Don't pet a *service dog* while it's working.

gloss: A dog bred and trained to pull a sled over snow.
examples: *Sled dogs* can run a hundred miles a day.
Each *sled dog* eats an enormous amount.
The *sled dog* team pulled up the trail.

gloss: An adult male cat.
examples: A big orange *tomcat* lives under the porch.
*Tomcats* fight over territory.
The *tomcat* has a torn ear.

gloss: An affectionate word for a cat, especially a young one.
examples: Come here, *kitty*.
The kids named the *kitty* Waffles.
Two *kitties* were curled up in the box.

gloss: A friendly, informal word for a dog.
examples: That *pooch* has the run of the house.
Take the *pooch* out before bed.
A couple of *pooches* were waiting outside the store.

gloss: A cat with a striped or blotched coat.
examples: The orange *tabby* sleeps in the window.
*Tabbies* have an M-shaped mark on the forehead.
We adopted a gray *tabby* from the shelter.

gloss: A cat that lives wild and avoids people.
examples: A colony of *feral cats* lives behind the diner.
The *feral cat* won't let anyone near her.
Volunteers trap and neuter *feral cats*.

gloss: A cat, or any animal of the cat family.
examples: The clinic treats both canines and *felines*.
A *feline* landed silently on the fence.
*Felines* sleep most of the day.

gloss: A dog, or any animal of the dog family.
examples: The vaccine protects *canines* against several viruses.
This unit works with a *canine* partner.
*Canines* and felines need different diets.
contrast: *Canine* is also the name of the pointed tooth on each side of your front teeth.

gloss: A small orange fish commonly kept as a pet.
examples: The *goldfish* outlived the dog.
We won two *goldfish* at the fair.
Don't overfeed the *goldfish*.
contrast: The plural is *goldfish*, unchanged — not goldfishes.

gloss: A tiny brightly colored tropical fish kept in tanks.
examples: The *guppies* had babies again.
A single *guppy* costs about two dollars.
*Guppies* are a good fish for a first tank.

gloss: A small desert rodent with long back legs, kept as a pet.
examples: The *gerbil* runs on his wheel all night.
*Gerbils* need deep bedding to dig in.
Her class keeps a *gerbil* in the corner.
contrast: The g sounds like j: JUR-buhl.

gloss: A small South American rodent with extremely soft gray fur.
examples: A *chinchilla* has the softest fur of any animal.
*Chinchillas* bathe in dust, not water.
The *chinchilla* chewed through the cage bars.

gloss: A small gray Australian parrot with a crest and orange cheek patches.
examples: The *cockatiel* whistles the same three notes all day.
*Cockatiels* can learn to talk a little.
Her *cockatiel* rides around on her shoulder.

gloss: The branch of farming that deals with raising and caring for livestock.
examples: He studied *animal husbandry* at the state college.
*Animal husbandry* covers feeding, breeding, and health.
The course includes basic *animal husbandry*.
contrast: Husbandry here has nothing to do with husbands; it means the care of farm animals.

gloss: The coming together of a male and female animal to produce young.
examples: *Mating* usually happens in early spring.
The pair were kept apart until *mating* season.
He wrote down the date of *mating*.

gloss: The time an animal carries its young before birth.
examples: *Gestation* in dogs is about nine weeks.
The cow is in the last month of *gestation*.
*Gestation* is shorter in smaller animals.

gloss: Moving a young animal from its mother's milk onto other food.
examples: The puppies are ready for *weaning* at four weeks.
*Weaning* went smoothly with this litter.
After *weaning*, they move on to solid food.

gloss: A large farm in the western US where cattle or horses are raised.
examples: They run a cattle *ranch* in Montana.
The *ranch* covers eight thousand acres.
Several *ranches* lost stock in the storm.

gloss: Someone who owns or runs a ranch.
examples: The *rancher* checks the herd every morning.
*Ranchers* were hit hard by the drought.
Her grandfather was a *rancher* in Wyoming.

gloss: A farm that keeps cows for their milk.
examples: He grew up on a *dairy farm* in Wisconsin.
The *dairy farm* milks two hundred cows.
Small *dairy farms* are disappearing.
contrast: Dairy is DAIR-ee; don't confuse it with diary, DY-uh-ree, the book you write in.

gloss: The open yard around a barn where farm animals move about.
examples: Chickens wandered around the *barnyard*.
The *barnyard* turns to mud every spring.
Both *barnyards* were fenced in.

gloss: A fenced yard where cattle are fattened on grain before slaughter.
examples: The steers spend their last months in a *feedlot*.
The *feedlot* holds ten thousand head.
*Feedlots* are common out on the plains.

gloss: The work of taking milk from cows, goats or sheep.
examples: *Milking* starts at four in the morning.
He does the evening *milking* by himself.
*Milking* twice a day is standard.

gloss: Driving and keeping together a group of animals.
examples: *Herding* is pure instinct for these dogs.
The border collie is bred for *herding*.
*Herding* the cattle downhill took all day.

gloss: Feeding on growing grass, or land used for that.
examples: The sheep were moved to fresh *grazing*.
*Grazing* is limited on public land.
There's good *grazing* on the north slope.

gloss: Dried food such as hay or corn stored for farm animals.
examples: They store *fodder* for the winter.
The barn is full of *fodder*.
Corn is grown here mainly as *fodder*.
contrast: Uncountable: some *fodder*, never 'a fodder'.

gloss: Green plants packed and fermented in a pit as winter cattle feed.
examples: The cows are fed *silage* through the winter.
He filled the pit with *silage*.
*Silage* smells sour, but the cattle love it.

gloss: A long open container that animals eat or drink from.
examples: The pigs crowded around the *trough*.
Fill the water *trough* before you leave.
The *troughs* freeze over in January.
contrast: The gh sounds like f: TRAWF.

gloss: A box or rack in a stable that holds hay for animals.
examples: The calf ate straight out of the *manger*.
Hay was piled in the *manger*.
Each stall has its own *manger*.
contrast: MAYN-jur — a different word from manager, MAN-uh-jur.

gloss: A separate space in a stable or barn for one animal.
examples: Each horse has its own *stall*.
He mucked out the *stall* every morning.
All twelve *stalls* were full.

gloss: A small fenced field where horses are kept or exercised.
examples: Turn the mare out into the *paddock*.
The *paddock* fence needs repair.
The horses graze in the lower *paddock*.

gloss: A fenced enclosure for holding cattle or horses.
examples: They drove the cattle into the *corral*.
The *corral* gate had been left open.
Both *corrals* were built from cedar posts.
contrast: Stressed on the second syllable, kuh-RAL — not the same as coral, KOR-uhl, from the sea.

gloss: A place where eggs are hatched under controlled conditions.
examples: The chicks come from a *hatchery* in Iowa.
The *hatchery* ships day-old chicks.
Two *hatcheries* supply the whole region.

gloss: A heated box that keeps eggs at the right temperature until they hatch.
examples: The eggs stay in the *incubator* for twenty-one days.
He built an *incubator* out of an old cooler.
The *incubators* have to hold a steady temperature.

gloss: A young cow that has not yet had a calf.
examples: The *heifer* will calve in the spring.
He sold six *heifers* at auction.
That *heifer* has never been bred.
contrast: Spelled with ei but pronounced HEF-ur.

gloss: A male horse that has been castrated.
examples: She rides a bay *gelding*.
*Geldings* are usually calmer than stallions.
The *gelding* is fifteen years old.

gloss: An animal between one and two years old.
examples: The *yearling* is already taller than its mother.
*Yearlings* sell well at this auction.
He bought a *yearling* colt.

gloss: A man who herds and tends cattle on horseback.
examples: A *cowboy* rode out to check the fence line.
*Cowboys* still work cattle on horseback here.
Her father was a *cowboy* in Wyoming.

gloss: A person who rides horses in races as a job.
examples: The *jockey* weighed in at a hundred and twelve pounds.
*Jockeys* have to keep their weight down.
The *jockey* pulled the horse up early.

gloss: A person whose job is looking after sheep.
examples: The *shepherd* moved the flock at dawn.
*Shepherds* spend months out with the sheep.
An old *shepherd* pointed us up the trail.
contrast: The h in the middle is silent: SHEP-urd.

gloss: A worker who feeds horses and cleans out a stable.
examples: The *stable hand* feeds the horses at six.
He worked as a *stable hand* through high school.
Two *stable hands* muck out the barn each day.

gloss: A curved iron plate nailed to the bottom of a horse's hoof.
examples: The *horseshoe* had worked loose.
*Horseshoes* are nailed into the hard part of the hoof.
She hung a *horseshoe* over the door for luck.

gloss: A craftsman who trims horses' hooves and fits their shoes.
examples: The *farrier* comes out every six weeks.
A good *farrier* is hard to find.
*Farriers* trim hooves as well as fit shoes.

gloss: The straps around a horse's head that the reins attach to.
examples: He slipped the *bridle* over the horse's head.
The *bridle* hangs by the stall door.
All the *bridles* need oiling.
contrast: *Bridle* sounds exactly like bridal, which means having to do with a wedding.

gloss: A long strap running from the bridle that the rider holds to steer.
examples: She pulled on the left *rein*.
Hold the *reins* in both hands.
One *rein* had snapped clean through.
contrast: *Rein* sounds like rain and like reign — three different words.

gloss: One of the two metal loops hanging from a saddle for the rider's feet.
examples: His boot slipped out of the *stirrup*.
Shorten the *stirrups* before you mount.
One *stirrup* hangs lower than the other.

gloss: A simple headpiece with a rope, used to lead an animal.
examples: Put a *halter* on him before you lead him out.
The *halter* was hanging on the fence post.
The *halters* are labeled with each horse's name.

gloss: A small metal point on a rider's heel, used to urge a horse on.
examples: The rider touched the horse with a *spur*.
*Spurs* should be used lightly, if at all.
One *spur* had come off in the dirt.

gloss: A numbered plastic tag clipped into a farm animal's ear.
examples: Every calf gets an *ear tag* with a number.
The *ear tag* fell out somewhere in the field.
*Ear tags* let you track each animal.

gloss: The low steady sound a contented cat makes.
examples: The cat let out a low *purr*.
You could hear his *purr* across the room.
Her *purrs* got louder when I scratched her chin.

gloss: The crying sound a cat makes.
examples: A thin *meow* came from under the porch.
She answered with a single *meow*.
The *meows* got louder around dinnertime.

gloss: A low threatening sound made in the throat by an animal.
examples: A low *growl* came from behind the couch.
He gave a warning *growl* and backed away.
The *growls* stopped when she recognized me.

gloss: A sharp sound like a long s, made by an angry cat or a snake.
examples: The cat backed away with a *hiss*.
That *hiss* means leave her alone.
There were *hisses* from both cats.

gloss: A long loud cry made by a dog or wolf.
examples: A long *howl* woke the whole street.
The dog let out a mournful *howl*.
You could hear *howls* from the kennel.

gloss: A high complaining sound made by a dog wanting something.
examples: The puppy let out a *whine* at the door.
That *whine* means he needs to go out.
We ignored the *whines* until morning.
contrast: For most Americans *whine* sounds exactly like wine.

gloss: A short sharp cry of pain or surprise from a dog.
examples: The dog gave a sharp *yelp* when I stepped on his tail.
A *yelp* came from the yard.
There were a couple of *yelps*, then silence.

gloss: An angry growl made with the teeth showing.
examples: He curled his lip in a *snarl*.
The *snarl* was enough to back the stranger off.
*Snarls* came from both sides of the fence.

gloss: A quick side-to-side movement of an animal's tail.
examples: He greeted us with a *wag* of his tail.
A slow *wag* means something different from a fast one.
Her tail gave a couple of *wags*.

gloss: The long high call a horse makes.
examples: The horse let out a *neigh*.
A *neigh* carried across the field.
*Neighs* came from the far end of the barn.
contrast: Sounds just like nay; the gh is silent.

gloss: The deep call a cow makes.
examples: A long *moo* came from the barn.
The calf answered with a soft *moo*.
You could hear the *moos* at feeding time.
